source: ECMA-262 (JavaScript RegExp), regular-expressions.info flavor guide, and engine documentation

entries.title: ECMAScript RegExp semantics (ECMA-262)
entries.body: ECMA-262 defines JavaScript's RegExp as an NFA backtracking engine. Flags: g (global), i (ignoreCase), m (multiline), s (dotAll), u (Unicode), y (sticky). ES2018 added lookbehind and named groups; ES2024 added the /v flag (unicodeSets) with string-set notation and difference/intersubtraction of classes. JavaScript has NO possessive quantifiers (a*+) and NO atomic groups (?>...). Invalid backreferences throw SyntaxError at construction; unmatched groups in replacement are treated as empty.

entries.title: Unicode mode and property escapes (ECMA-262 /u and /v)
entries.body: In Unicode mode (u flag, or implicitly v), the pattern is parsed as code points, \u{...} escapes are allowed, and Unicode property escapes \p{...} become available (e.g. \p{Script=Greek}, \p{Emoji}). The /v flag (ES2024) extends this with set operations on character classes. Without u, surrogates and astral characters are matched as two code units, producing silently wrong matches on non-BMP text. Always test multilingual input in u/v mode.

entries.title: PCRE backtracking, lookaround, atomic groups & possessive quantifiers
entries.body: PCRE/PCRE2 is a backtracking engine that supports lookahead (?=..), lookbehind (?<=..), atomic groups (?>..) and possessive quantifiers (a*+, a++). Atomic groups and possessives eliminate backtracking for a sub-expression and are the primary ReDoS mitigation when you must stay on a backtracking engine. Without them, nested/overlapping quantifiers can blow up exponentially. PCRE2 also offers JIT compilation and match-time limits for defense in depth.

entries.title: Go regexp uses RE2 — linear time, no backrefs/lookaround
entries.body: Go's regexp package is backed by RE2, a DFA-based engine that guarantees linear time and CANNOT suffer catastrophic backtracking. The trade-off: it has no backreferences and no lookaround ((?<=) / (?=)). Patterns that rely on capture-backrefs or lookaround fail to compile under Go. Prefer Go's regexp for any untrusted input — it is the safest default against ReDoS.

entries.title: Rust `regex` crate — finite automaton, no backrefs/lookaround
entries.body: The Rust `regex` crate compiles to a finite automaton and runs in linear time; it deliberately omits backreferences and lookaround to preserve that guarantee. For backrefs/lookaround use the `fancy-regex` crate, which is NOT linear-time and reintroduces ReDoS exposure. The standard crate's syntax is a restricted subset of PCRE; consult its docs for supported features before porting a pattern from Python/PCRE/JS.

entries.title: Python `re` backtracking, no possessive/atomic
entries.body: CPython's `re` module is a backtracking engine. It supports lookaround and named groups ((?P<name>..)) but has NO possessive quantifiers and NO atomic groups. To avoid ReDoS on untrusted input, either bound input length, rewrite nested quantifiers, or switch to Google's `regex`/`re2` bindings (`google-re2`) for linear-time matching. Note `re` is not ISO 3166 or Unicode-collation aware by default.
